Confirmed claim c2 (in_scope, scope evidence citing problem.txt's tie clause plus the declared power-of-two column domain) shows the kernel does not implement that rule. Probe t16, bound directly to c2, gives three independent in-domain constructions plus a control: (A) exhaustive duplicate-max pairs at N=2,4,8,16,32 returned the HIGHER tied index in 156/651 cases (23.96%), with 0 non-tied returns and rows_where_value_still_max == pairs at every N; (B) quantized rows (randint(0,L), L in {2,4,8}) at N=2,8,64,256,1024 gave 1098/3840 mismatches vs torch.argmax with higher_than_ref==1098 and lower_than_ref==0 in all 15 configurations and value_still_max==3840, i.e. the returned element is always a true row max so this is purely a tie-break-direction defect, not a value error; (C) the misroute survives the contract's batch mean-pooling (69 misrouted tokens, pooled rel-L2 0.41, max abs diff 0.31), so it is not diluted below any plausible tolerance; (D) a strictly-distinct control had 0 mismatches, isolating the defect to exact ties. The source mechanism matches: kernel.py:24 `cond = (left > right) != flip` is true on exact equality when flip=DESCENDING=1 (set line 69, threaded line 56) and kernel.py:26 XOR-swaps the ids for those lanes, making the descending network anti-stable. The reference behavior is fully specified (lowest index), so this is not a reference-undefined or unspecified-tie-break case that the safe-harbor rules would excuse; the contract explicitly legislates the exact case that fails. c1 (ordering machinery for distinct values) is rebutted by t8 (640/640 rows exact argmax, valid permutations, non-increasing gathered scores at N=2..1024), which sharpens rather than weakens the finding. Generalization notes set aside as non-decisive because problem.txt does not require them: k>1 tie ordering, non-float32 dtypes through the line-20 bitcast, inf/NaN through the lines 11-12 mask-sum reduction, and non-power-of-two N.
